# Coordinated assembly of the multilayered cell envelope of Gram-negative bacteria

**Authors:** Elayne M. Fivenson; Laurent Dubois; Thomas G. Bernhardt

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Microbiology, Blavatnik Institute, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115. | 2Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Boston, United States.

## Abstract

Bacteria surround themselves with complex cell envelopes to maintain their integrity and protect against external insults. The envelope of Gram-negative organisms is multilayered with two membranes sandwiching the periplasmic space that contains the peptidoglycan cell wall. Understanding how this complicated surface architecture is assembled during cell growth and division is a major fundamental problem in microbiology. Additionally, because the envelope is an important antibiotic target and determinant of intrinsic antibiotic resistance, understanding the mechanisms governing its assembly is relevant to therapeutic development. In the last several decades, most of the factors required to build the Gram-negative envelope have been identified. However, surprisingly little is known about how the biogenesis of the different cell surface layers is coordinated. Here, we provide an overview of recent work that is beginning to uncover the links connecting the different envelope biosynthetic pathways and assembly machines to ensure uniform envelope growth.

## Introduction

Many significant human pathogens such as Escherichia coli and other enterobacteria, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii belong to the Proteobacteria phylum and are often referred to simply as Gram-negative bacteria based on their staining properties. Infections with these organisms are becoming increasingly difficult to treat in part due to the high intrinsic resistance to antibiotics conferred by their complex cell surface[1]. This diderm envelope consists of two membranes: an inner membrane (IM) and an outer membrane (OM). The compartment in between these two membranes is called the periplasm, which contains a thin layer of peptidoglycan (PG). The IM is a typical phospholipid (PL) bilayer whereas the OM is asymmetric with PL in the inner leaflet and an outer leaflet composed of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Fig. 1). LPS consists of the lipid A glycolipid attached to a core oligosaccharide and, depending on the organism, a longer, O-antigen (O-Ag) polysaccharide chain (for reviews, please see [2,3]). Lateral interactions between LPS molecules provide the barrier function to the OM, preventing entry of both large polar molecules and small hydrophobic molecules [3,4]. The PG layer fortifies the IM and prevents osmotic lysis. It also confers bacterial cells with their characteristic shape[5,6]. These roles were once thought to be exclusive to the PG cell wall, but recent findings show that the OM also contributes to the mechanical stability of the envelope [7–10] and cell shape[11*] in addition to its role as a permeability barrier.

Over the last several decades, most of the biosynthesis pathways and protein machineries that assemble the Gram-negative cell envelope have been identified and characterized. The only major factors that remained elusive were the systems that transport PLs from the IM to the OM, but recent work indicates that AsmA-like proteins are likely functioning in this capacity[12**, 13**, 14**, 15**]. Now that we have a clear picture of the players involved, the next major challenge for the field is to determine how the biogenesis of different envelope layers is regulated and coordinated to promote uniform surface growth. The control mechanisms involved likely operate during the synthesis of individual envelope building blocks and at the level of the multiprotein machines that carry out the final assembly steps that form the different layers. We will summarize recent progress in understanding both types of control processes.

## Pathways for envelope subunit synthesis use common precursors

Synthesis pathways for major envelope components use common precursors (Fig. 2). The activated sugar UDP-N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc) is used to form the carbohydrate components of lipid A [16] and the PG cell wall [17]. Acyl-acyl carrier protein (acyl-ACP) is the source of acyl chains for both LPS [16] and PL synthesis [18], but the two pathways siphon off chains of different length from the fatty acid synthesis cycle. Shorter acyl groups (C12 and C14-OH) are used for LPS synthesis whereas longer chains (C16 and C18) enter the PL synthesis pathway. Most bacteria only encode one pathway for synthesizing the essential PL precursor lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) using the PlsX and PlsY enzymes [19,20]. PlsX converts acyl-ACP into acyl-phosphate (acyl-P). PlsY then transfers the acyl chain from acyl-P to glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P) to form LPA [19]. Notably, E. coli and many other ɣ-proteobacteria encode a second LPA synthesis enzyme called PlsB that is homologous to the enzyme used by eukaryotes [20–23]. PlsB directly transfers an acyl group from acyl-ACP to G3P to form LPA[22]. It is the essential and major enzyme for LPA synthesis in E. coli. Regardless of the pathway used, the LPA produced is the substrate for PlsC, which adds the second acyl chain to form phosphatidic acid (PA), which is used to add headgroups for mature PL production[22].

Because cell growth and surface expansion are necessarily coupled, the pathways that supply envelope building blocks have long been thought to be regulated by growth rate, and many points of control have been identified and studied over the years, especially within the pathways for membrane biogenesis[24–31]. Additionally, the use of common precursors has also led to the idea that control mechanisms must exist to coordinate the different synthesis pathways to prevent imbalanced flux in one direction from causing the potentially toxic overproduction of one component at the expense of causing a damaging deficit in another. The regulation and coordination of these processes does not always require a complicated multiprotein control mechanism, at least during steady-state growth. For example, the allosteric regulation of PlsB and negative feedback on the ACC complex by long-chain acyl-ACP[32] has been shown to be sufficient for adjusting PL synthesis to steady-state growth rate and balancing PL and LPS production[33**]. However, it is probably not often that bacteria in the wild experience a constant supply of nutrients. Fluctuating conditions likely necessitate additional levels of control such as those that have been observed to regulate LPS synthesis [24, 25, 34**, 35*, 36*, 37*, 38*, 39*, 40*, 41*] and potentially coordinate it with the production of other envelope components.

## All roads lead to LpxC, a key node of envelope synthesis regulation

The synthesis of the lipid A moiety of LPS begins with the acylation of UDP-N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc) by LpxA[16,42]. This reaction is reversible, and it is the deacetylation of the LpxA product catalyzed by LpxC that is the committed step[43,44]. LpxC is therefore a major point of regulation for the control of envelope biogenesis. In E. coli and related enterobacteria, LpxC is has long been known to be degraded by the protease FtsH [41*,45–48] and its adapter LapB (YciM) [49,50]. However, it remained unclear for some time how LpxC proteolysis is controlled to regulate LPS synthesis. Several years ago, we and others discovered that the essential protein YejM (PbgA, LapC) modulates LpxC proteolysis by FtsH-LapB[35*, 36*, 37*, 38*, 39*, 40*, 41*]. The combined results support a model [39*] in which YejM modulates LpxC proteolysis to coordinate LPS synthesis with its transport to the OM by the Lpt pathway [51] (Fig. 3A). When LPS synthesis is matched with the rate of OM assembly, LPS concentration in the outer leaflet of the IM will be low. In this condition, YejM binds to LapB and prevents its ability to recruit LpxC to FtsH for degradation. However, when LPS synthesis exceeds transport capacity, the concentration of LPS in the IM will rise, promoting LPS binding to YejM at a site that overlaps with the LapB interface[37*,41*]. The LPS-YejM interaction therefore displaces LapB, allowing it to trigger increased turnover of LpxC by FtsH, ultimately reducing LPS synthesis to balance synthesis and transport[37*,41*]. Thus, a major role of the YejM-FtsH-LapB system appears to be preventing the toxic accumulation of LPS in the IM[39*].

LpxC accumulation in E. coli also appears to be sensitive to the accumulation of PL cleavage products generated by the OM phospholipase PldA [52*]. When PLs invade the outer leaflet of the OM, they must be removed to maintain OM barrier function. Removal of these PLs is accomplished by a partially redundant set of OM asymmetry factors: PagP[53], the Mla system[54], and PldA[55]. The action of PldA on PLs in the outer leaflet of the OM generates LPA and a free fatty acid. It is the uptake of the released fatty acids and their conversion to acyl-CoA molecules that has been associated with the stabilization of LpxC[52*]. Although the mechanism of LpxC stabilization induced via the generation of acyl-CoAs remains unclear, it suggests that cells use the presence of PLs in the outer leaflet of the OM as a signal that insufficient levels of LPS are being made to cover the OM and that synthesis should be increased.

Unlike E. coli, LpxC in P. aeruginosa (PaLpxC) is not proteolyzed by FtsH[34**,56]. Instead, an interaction with PaMurA, the enzyme that catalyzes the committed step of PG synthesis, is required for LpxC activity in this organism[34**]. Bioinformatic and biochemical analysis of MurA and LpxC from other organisms indicates that this mode of LpxC regulation is likely to be conserved in many proteobacteria outside of the enterobacteria like E. coli[34**]. Why P. aeruginosa and other proteobacteria utilize this LpxC regulatory mechanism whereas E. coli and its relatives use the proteolytic control system remains unclear, but differences in niche and carbon source preference likely play a role. Nevertheless, the connection between the committed enzymes of both LPS and PG pathways represents an attractive mechanism for coordinating PG and OM biogenesis in the organisms that use this regulatory system (Fig. 3B).

## Links between OM and PG expansion

Because it is a continuous matrix surrounding the cell, the PG layer must be cleaved to open space in the network for the insertion of new material during growth. Enzymes that cleave the PG must be tightly regulated to prevent aberrant cleavage and cell lysis[57]. The activity of these factors must presumably also be coordinated with the activity of PG synthases that “fill” the voids created by PG cleavage, and this expansion of the wall must in turn be connected to IM and OM growth. We have much to learn about the mechanisms that orchestrate this coordinated expansion of the envelope, but recent studies have provided us with a glimpse of the connections involved.

In E. coli, one of the major “space making” enzymes is the endopeptidase MepS that cleaves peptide crosslinks in the PG layer[58]. MepS is a lipoprotein localized in the inner leaflet of the OM. Like LpxC, its accumulation in cells is also controlled by regulated proteolysis, but in this case, it is degraded by the periplasmic protease Prc (Tsp) and the adapter NlpI[59]. An investigation into the control of MepS turnover by Pcr/NlpI revealed that it is negatively regulated by yet to be identified signals generated by the OM asymmetry factors[60**]. The results support a model in which transient areas of broken OM asymmetry arise during times of robust membrane biogenesis, causing the generation of molecular cues like PL cleavage products by the OM asymmetry factors, which then negatively regulate NlpI to promote MepS stabilization, allowing PG expansion to keep pace with OM growth [60**]. This model is attractive because it provides a potential explanation for previous findings showing that fatty acid/PL availability determines cell size[61,62]. Furthermore, it is unlikely to be a coincidence that some of the same signals controlling MepS stability also impact LpxC levels. Thus, further studies of MepS and LpxC proteolysis may reveal still more connections between OM and PG growth.

Unlike the IM, where phospholipids and proteins can diffuse [63], the motion of LPS molecules and β-Barrel outer membrane proteins (OMPs) is restricted due to the “crosslinking” of adjacent LPS molecules in the outer leaflet of the OM by coordinated cations like Mg2+ and Ca2+[64,65]. Newly inserted LPS and OMPs therefore remain relatively fixed in the positions where they are inserted in the OM[64,66]. Imaging studies have found that E. coli OMPs are inserted throughout the cell-cylinder as well as at the cell division site, but not at the poles[66]. Notably, this insertion pattern mirrors that observed for sites of PG insertion into the matrix[67,68], suggesting that the two processes may be linked. Recent work suggests that this may indeed be the case. When PG is synthesized, the newly inserted material is enriched in glycan chains with attached pentapeptides[6]. However, due to the crosslinking process and the action of enzymes called carboxypeptidases, the pentapeptides are rapidly converted to tetrapeptides via removal of the terminal D-alanine[6]. It was found that PG tetrapeptides bind to the BAM complex that inserts OMPs in the OM and blocks its OMP foldase activity in a purified system[69**]. PG pentapeptides, on the other hand, have low affinity for the BAM machine. These findings therefore support a model in which OMP assembly may be coordinated with sites of PG expansion to couple OM growth with PG expansion[69**]. How LPS insertion would be similarly coordinated remains unclear, but since the OM component of the Lpt transport system, LptD, is an OMP[51], coordination of PG and LPS insertion may be a “built-in” feature of the PG-OMP connection.

## The curious case of YhcB

Another potential connector linking PG and LPS synthesis in E. coli is YhcB (ZapG, LapD), an inner membrane protein conserved among the ɣ-proteobacteria[70]. Mutants in yhcB were identified in several different screens for mutants with temperature sensitive or envelope defective phenotypes[71–73*]. Loss of YhcB function has also been found to be synthetically lethal with defects in the RodZ component of the PG elongation machinery (the Rod complex/elongasome)[73*,74] as well as with mutants defective for other aspects of PG synthesis and recycling and OM biogenesis[73*]. Mutants lacking YhcB have a pleotropic phenotype, displaying defects in the OM permeability barrier, cell morphology and division defects, and excess PLs[70,73*,75,76]. YhcB has been found to interact with many different proteins implicated in envelope biogenesis, including: RodZ and other components of the Rod system[70,74], proteins involved in PL synthesis[76], YciS(LapA) [70,74,76], LapB[76], and FtsH[76]. All these findings have led to the idea that YhcB forms some kind of central interaction/regulatory hub connecting many different aspects of envelope assembly. However, the physiological relevance of many of the interactions involving YhcB remains to be determined. It is also unclear which phenotypes of yhcB mutants are proximal verses downstream consequences of an initial problem. Nevertheless, YhcB is clearly playing an important role in envelope biogenesis and may form part of one or more regulatory nodes coordinating the biogenesis of the different surface layers.

## Sharing the polyprenyl lipid carrier

Surface glycans like PG, O-Ag, and capsule are polymerized from monomeric building blocks attached to polyprenyl lipids like undecaprenyl phosphate (C55P) [77,78]. The concentration of this carrier is limiting, suggesting that there must be mechanisms to efficiently distribute the carrier between competing pathways. Otherwise, excess steady-state accumulation of monomer units for one polymer will sequester the limiting carrier, indirectly inhibiting the production of other glycans and causing defects in envelope assembly[79–81]. Despite the importance of efficient carrier utilization for the balanced synthesis of different surface glycans, the underlying mechanism has remained elusive. Recent work studying the biogenesis of lipid linked PG precursors by the conserved MraY protein suggests that feedback regulation is likely playing a role [82**].

MraY catalyzes the first membrane-localized step of PG synthesis. It transfers an N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc) sugar with its attached pentapeptide (p5) from UDP-MurNAc-p5 to the C55P carrier, forming the intermediate called lipid I [83]. A GlcNAc sugar from UDP-GlcNAc is then added to this molecule to form lipid II, the final PG precursor[84]. Once made, lipid II must be flipped to place the disaccharide-peptide moiety on the outer face of the membrane for polymerization into PG. Following each step of polymerization, C55-pyrophosphate is released, dephosphorylated to C55-P, and the lipid carrier is recycled back to the cytoplasmic face of the IM by DedA-family and other transporters [85**–87**], where it can be reused for a new round of synthesis lipid recycling.

Genetic, biochemical, and biophysical studies support a model that MraY is feedback inhibited by the accumulation of lipid II in the flipped/periplasmic orientation [82**]. This feedback regulation model is attractive because it provides a straightforward means of preventing lipid II accumulation beyond levels needed by the PG polymerases. If more lipid II is produced than can be used to make PG, the steady state level of lipid II will increase, triggering a decline in MraY activity via feedback inhibition that reduces the supply until homeostasis is reestablished. Importantly, MraY belongs to the widely distributed polyprenyl-phosphate N-acetylhexosamine 1-phosphate transferase (PNPT) superfamily of enzymes, many of which are involved in initiating the membrane steps of O-Ag and capsule synthesis [78]. Thus, control of other PNPT enzymes by a similar feedback circuit would provide a mechanism to ensure that pathways competing for C55P share it equitably.

## Conclusion

Decades of work by many labs have identified most of the enzymes and assembly machines that build the Gram-negative envelope. However, surprisingly little is known about how the synthesis of the different cell surface layers is coordinated to ensure uniform surface growth. Recent work is starting to reveal some of these mechanisms, but there remains much to be learned. The insights provided from future work in this area will not only teach us how cells construct their surface but will also identify new ways to disrupt the surface assembly process to aid the development of new classes of antibacterial agents.
